claim: An AWS account can create up to 10,000 general purpose buckets by default; you request a higher quota in the Service Quotas console.
question: How many general purpose buckets can one AWS account create by default, and can the quota be raised?

evidence.quote: By default, you can create up to 10,000 general purpose buckets per AWS account. To request a quota increase for general purpose buckets, visit the [Service Quotas console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/servicequotas/home/services/s3/quotas/).

note: Raised from 100 to 10,000 in November 2024 (What's New 2024-11-14 in the change feed); the change lens adds the dated change.

claim: Unpaginated ListBuckets requests are only supported for accounts at the default general purpose bucket quota of 10,000; an account with an approved quota above 10,000 must send paginated ListBuckets requests.
question: What changes for ListBuckets when an account's general purpose bucket quota is raised above the default?

values.display: default general purpose bucket quota of 10,000
values.spoken: default quota of ten thousand buckets

evidence.quote: Unpaginated `ListBuckets` requests are only supported for AWS accounts set to the default general purpose bucket quota of 10,000. If you have an approved general purpose bucket quota above 10,000, you must send paginated `ListBuckets` requests to list your account’s buckets.

claim: A bucket has no maximum size and no limit on the number of objects it can store; you can keep all objects in one bucket, but a bucket cannot be created inside another bucket.
question: Is there a maximum bucket size or a maximum number of objects per bucket?

values.display: no limit on the number of objects
values.spoken: no limit on the number of objects

evidence.quote: There is no max bucket size or limit to the number of objects that you can store in a bucket. You can store all of your objects in a single bucket, or you can organize them across several buckets. However, you can't create a bucket from within another bucket.

claim: After you create a bucket, you cannot change its name or its AWS Region, and bucket ownership cannot be transferred to another account.
question: Can a bucket's name, Region or owning account be changed after creation?

values.display: can't change its name or Region
values.spoken: cannot change the name or the Region

evidence.quote: When you create a bucket, you choose its name and the AWS Region to create it in. After you create a bucket, you can't change its name or Region.
An Amazon S3 general purpose bucket is owned by the AWS account that created it. Bucket ownership is not transferable to another account.

claim: A single S3 object can be up to 50 TB in size; objects range from zero bytes to 50 TB. Until December 2, 2025 the maximum was 5 TB.
question: What is the maximum size of a single S3 object?

evidence.quote: You store these objects in one or more buckets, and each object can be up to 50 TB in size.
An object value can be any sequence of bytes. Objects can range in size from zero to 50 TB.

| [Large object support](#WhatsNew) | Amazon S3 has increased the maximum size of an object you can store in an S3 bucket from 5 TB to 50 TB. For uploading these larger objects, you must implement the Multipart Upload REST API to upload objects in parts, and when downloading these objects, use concurrent `GetObject` requests, as single GET requests are limited to 5 TB. For more information, see [Uploading objects](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/upload-objects.html) and [Downloading objects](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/download-objects.html). | December 2, 2025 |

note: Raised from 5 TB on December 2, 2025; older exam material assumes 5 TB. Single GET requests are still limited to 5 TB per the same row.

claim: The exact maximum object size is 53.7 TB (48.8 TiB), set by the multipart limits of 10,000 parts of 5 GiB each; AWS documentation commonly rounds this to 50 TB.
question: Where does the 50 TB object size limit come from, and what is the exact figure?

evidence.quote: While Amazon S3 documentation commonly references 50 TB object size limit, the actual maximum object size is 53.7 TB (48.8 TiB). This limit is determined by multipart upload constraints: 10,000 maximum parts x 5 GiB per part = 50,000 GiB (53.7 TB)

claim: A single PUT operation can upload one object of up to 5 GB; larger objects need multipart upload.
question: What is the largest object that one PUT request can upload?

qualifiers.condition: single operation through the SDKs, REST API or AWS CLI

evidence.quote: With a single `PUT` operation, you can upload a single object up to 5 GB in size.
Using the multipart upload API operation, you can upload a single large object, up to 50 TB in size.

claim: The S3 console can upload a file of up to 160 GB; a larger file needs the AWS CLI, an SDK or the REST API.
question: What is the largest file the S3 console can upload?

qualifiers.scope: per file uploaded in the S3 console

evidence.quote: The maximum size of a file that you can upload by using the Amazon S3 console is 160 GB. To upload a file larger than 160 GB, use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or Amazon S3 REST API.

claim: AWS calls multipart upload a best practice for objects of 100 MB or larger, instead of a single-operation upload.
question: From what object size does AWS recommend multipart upload?

evidence.quote: It's a best practice to use multipart upload for objects that are 100 MB or larger instead of uploading them in a single operation.
In general, when your object size reaches 100 MB, you should consider using multipart uploads instead of uploading the object in a single operation.

claim: Multipart upload works for objects from 5 MB to 50 TB in size.
question: What object size range does multipart upload support?

qualifiers.scope: per object uploaded with multipart upload

evidence.quote: You can use a multipart upload for objects from 5 MB to 50 TB in size.

claim: A started multipart upload has no expiry: you must explicitly complete or stop it, and its parts can be uploaded independently, in any order, and in parallel.
question: Does an unfinished multipart upload expire on its own?

qualifiers.condition: unless a lifecycle rule aborts incomplete multipart uploads

evidence.quote: After you initiate a multipart upload, there is no expiry; you must explicitly complete or stop the multipart upload.
These object parts can be uploaded independently, in any order, and in parallel.

claim: A presigned URL created in the S3 console can be valid for between 1 minute and 12 hours from the time of creation.
question: What is the longest a presigned URL made in the S3 console can stay valid?

qualifiers.scope: per presigned URL created in the S3 console

evidence.quote: When using the console the maximum expiration time for a presigned URL is 12 hours from the time of creation.
If you create a presigned URL with the Amazon S3 console, the expiration time can be set between 1 minute and 12 hours.

claim: A presigned URL created with the AWS CLI or an SDK can be valid for up to 7 days from the time of creation (Signature Version 4).
question: What is the longest a presigned URL made with the CLI or an SDK can stay valid?

qualifiers.scope: per presigned URL created with the AWS CLI or SDKs
qualifiers.condition: AWS Signature Version 4; long-lived IAM user credentials

evidence.quote: If you use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs, the expiration time can be set as high as 7 days.
When you use the AWS CLI, the maximum expiration time for a presigned URL is 7 days from the time of creation.
**IAM user** – Valid up to 7 days when you're using AWS Signature Version 4.

claim: A presigned URL made with temporary credentials expires when those credentials expire, even if the URL was given a later expiration time; a role-based URL ends with the role session.
question: What happens to a presigned URL when the credentials that signed it expire before the URL's own expiration time?

evidence.quote: If you created a presigned URL using a temporary credential, the URL expires when the credential expires. In general, a presigned URL expires when the credential you used to create it is revoked, deleted, or deactivated. This is true even if the URL was created with a later expiration time.
**IAM role credentials** – The presigned URL expires when the role session expires, even if you specify a longer expiration time.

claim: A presigned URL signed with the role credentials of an EC2 instance is valid only for the duration of those role credentials, typically 6 hours.
question: How long is a presigned URL valid when an EC2 instance role signs it?

qualifiers.condition: signed with the IAM role credentials of an EC2 instance

evidence.quote: **IAM role credentials used by Amazon EC2 instances** – Valid for the duration of the role credentials (typically 6 hours).

claim: The S3 console can generate a presigned URL for sharing an object of up to 5 TB.
question: How large an object can the S3 console share through a presigned URL?

qualifiers.scope: per object shared with a console-made presigned URL

evidence.quote: You can use the Amazon S3 console to generate a presigned URL for sharing an object up to 5 TB by following these steps.

claim: A bucket policy is limited to 20 KB in size; identity-based policies have the same 20 KB limit, so complex per-object permissions need access points or S3 Access Grants instead.
question: What is the maximum size of an S3 bucket policy?

evidence.quote: Only the bucket owner can associate a policy with a bucket. The permissions attached to the bucket apply to all of the objects in the bucket that are owned by the bucket owner. Bucket policies are limited to 20 KB in size.
Both bucket policies and identity-based policies have a 20 KB size limit. If your access permission requirements are complex, you might exceed this size limit.

claim: An AWS account can create up to 100 directory buckets per Region, with no limit on the number of objects in a bucket; contact Support to raise the quota.
question: How many directory buckets can one account create?

evidence.quote: You can create up to 100 directory buckets in each of your AWS accounts, with no limit on the number of objects that you can store in a bucket. Your bucket quota is applied to each Region in your AWS account. If your application requires increasing this limit, contact Support.

claim: A directory bucket in an Availability Zone with no request activity for at least 90 days becomes inactive and is temporarily inaccessible for reads and writes until a request reactivates it; storage charges continue.
question: What happens to a directory bucket that receives no requests for a long time?

qualifiers.scope: per directory bucket in an Availability Zone

evidence.quote: Directory buckets in Availability Zones that have no request activity for a period of at least 90 days transition to an inactive state. While in an inactive state, a directory bucket is temporarily inaccessible for reads and writes. Inactive buckets retain all storage, object metadata, and bucket metadata. Existing storage charges apply to inactive buckets.

claim: Restore requests from the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive and S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage classes are limited to 1,000 transactions per second per account; above that rate requests are throttled with a ThrottlingException, and S3 Batch Operations can restore many objects in one request.
question: How many restore requests per second does an account get for archived objects?

qualifiers.condition: RestoreObject requests for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive or S3 Intelligent-Tiering objects

evidence.quote: S3 Glacier supports restore requests at a rate of 1,000 transactions per second. If this rate is exceeded otherwise valid requests are throttled or rejected and Amazon S3 returns a `ThrottlingException` error. You can use S3 Batch Operations to retrieve many objects with a single request, which fully utilizes the restore request rate available in your account.

claim: S3 Glacier restores large datasets at up to 1–2 petabytes per day per customer account; any object larger than 5 terabytes restores at up to 300 megabytes per second, so a 50-terabyte S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval object could take up to 48 hours.
question: How fast can an account restore a very large archive, and why does a huge single object take longer?

values.spoken: one to two petabytes per day

qualifiers.condition: contact AWS Support for higher restoration limits

evidence.quote: After you initiate restore requests, S3 Glacier supports restoring large datasets at a throughput of up to 1–2 petabytes per day per customer account. For any retrieval option, objects larger than 5 terabytes will take longer to be restored with up to 300 megabytes per second of retrieval throughput. For example, a 50-terabyte S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval object could take up to 48 hours to complete. If you require increased restoration limits, you can contact AWS Support.

claim: One unit of provisioned capacity guarantees at least 3 Expedited retrievals every 5 minutes from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and up to 300 megabytes per second of retrieval throughput; without it, Expedited retrievals might not be accepted during periods of high demand.
question: What does one unit of S3 Glacier provisioned capacity give you, and what happens without it?

values.spoken: three expedited retrievals every five minutes

qualifiers.condition: Expedited retrievals from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval

evidence.quote: Each unit of capacity provides that at least three Expedited retrievals can be performed every 5 minutes, and it provides up to 300 megabytes per second of retrieval throughput.

Without provisioned capacity, Expedited retrievals might not be accepted during periods of high demand. For predictable, fast access to more of your data, consider using the [S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/storage-classes/glacier/instant-retrieval/) storage class.
